title: High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Quantized Models with Straight-Through Estimator
claim: Theoretical mean-field prediction matches finite-size simulation of training dynamics, which concentrate onto quantization levels over time.
layout: 4 panels in a row, left-to-right over training time, shared axes
description: A single row of four histogram-and-curve plots showing the weight density at training horizons τ=10, 25, 50 and 100, one per panel, with titles above. Each panel plots density against weight w, from about -5 to 5. Red histogram bars show the STE simulation. A smooth blue line shows the PDE prediction, and it follows the histograms closely. A legend in the first panel labels the two. At τ=10 the distribution is broad and roughly Gaussian with small peaks near 0 and 0.5. In later panels it narrows and concentrates into a sharp spike near w≈0.5 plus a smaller bump near 0. The y-axis scale grows from 0.6 to about 4 as the mass concentrates. The eye goes to the tall blue spikes.
caption: Comparison between STE simulations (red histograms) and the PDE prediction (blue curves) for the probability density µτ( ˆw|w∗= 1) at training horizons τ ∈{10, 25, 50, 100}. Simulations use d = 3,000, w∗= 1, and µ0 the standard Gaussian. Both the inputs and weights are quantized with ω = 2 and bit-width b = 2.
abstract: Quantized neural network training optimizes a discrete, non-differentiable objective. The straight-through estimator (STE) enables backpropagation through surrogate gradients and is widely used. While previous studies have primarily focused on the properties of surrogate gradients and their convergence, the influence of quantization hyperparameters, such as bit width and quantization range, on learning dynamics remains largely unexplored. We theoretically show that in the high-dimensional limit, STE dynamics converge to a deterministic ordinary differential equation. This reveals that STE training exhibits a plateau followed by a sharp drop in generalization error, with plateau length depending on the quantization range. A fixed-point analysis quantifies the asymptotic deviation from the unquantized linear model. We also extend analytical techniques for stochastic gradient descent to nonlinear transformations of weights and inputs.
